table.text: Ethics approval and consent to participate NHANES was approved by the National Center for Health Statistics Research Ethics Review Board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants; the relevant ethical approval protocol for the 1999-2004 survey cycles used in this analysis was Protocol #98-12.

As the study involved secondary analysis of existing de-identified data and did not involve direct interaction with human participants or access to identifiable private information, informed consent and Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval were waived.

Participants were classified into four phenotypes according to the 2026 Universal Definition of Heart Failure: no apparent risk, Stage A (at risk), Stage B (elevated NT-proBNP without self-reported HF), and Stage C (self-reported HF).
The HF-continuum phenotype was assigned cross-sectionally at baseline, and participants were subsequently followed for mortality.

Participants were eligible if they were aged ≥20 years at examination and had nonmissing self-reported HF status, complete examination and survey design variables, eligibility for mortality linkage, recorded follow-up time, and nonmissing core phenotype variables.

Consistent with the general principles of the Universal Definition and threshold approaches adopted in previous studies, [19] participants were classified as Stage B if their NT-proBNP concentration exceeded the 90th percentile of an age-and sex-specific reference distribution.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.305", Sentence = "Conversely, when Stage B was used as the reference, the comparison with Stage C showed no statistically significant difference in mortality (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71-1.11; p=0.305) (Table 3)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Objective: To develop and evaluate a biomarker-informed, computable phenotype of the heart failure (HF) continuum, aligned with 2026 AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF Expert Consensus, using NHANES and linked mortality data, and to determine whether this phenotype identifies subgroups with distinct mortality risks.
We analyzed 11,477 U.S. adults aged ≥20 years from the 1999-2004 NHANES cycles who participated in the surplus-sera biomarker substudy and were linked to National Death Index follow-up.

Participants were classified into four phenotypes according to the 2026 Universal Definition of Heart Failure: no apparent risk, Stage A (at risk), Stage B (elevated NT-proBNP without self-reported HF), and Stage C (self-reported HF).

Survey-weighted Kaplan-Meier curves and nested, multiply imputed Cox proportional hazards models, with sequential adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, and cardiometabolic covariates, were used to estimate associations with mortality.
Pairwise phenotype comparisons, standardized adjusted survival estimates, and restricted mean survival times were also calculated.
Incremental prognostic value was evaluated by comparing discrimination and reclassification metrics between the full phenotype and a conventional three-level model that excluded NT-proBNP.
Results: Weighted prevalences were 16.9%, 70.0%, 10.7%, and 2.4% for no apparent risk, Stage A, Stage B, and Stage C, respectively.
In fully adjusted models, the hazard ratios (HRs) relative to no apparent risk were 1.58 (95% CI, 1.08-2.30), 2.88 (95% CI, 2.00-4.16), and 2.56 (95% CI, 1.61-4.09), respectively.

Stage B was associated with significantly higher mortality risk than Stage A (HR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.62-2.07), whereas the difference between Stage C and Stage B was not statistically significant (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71-1.11).

The association for Stage B attenuated less across sequentially adjusted models than that for Stage C. Adjusted 10-year mortality risks were 15.2% for Stage B and 14.2% for Stage C. Incorporating Stage B into the conventional model yielded only marginal improvements in discrimination (ΔC-statistic, 0.002; 95% CI, 0.001-0.002).

Conclusion: A biomarker-informed phenotype of the HF continuum can be operationalized using national survey data and identifies a pre-HF subgroup with an adjusted mortality risk not significantly different from that of individuals with overt HF, despite only marginal gains in prognostic discrimination.

Heart failure (HF) affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults, and its prevalence is projected to increase. [1, 2] For decades, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) have conceptualized HF as a continuum encompassing asymptomatic individuals at risk (Stage A), structural or functional cardiac abnormalities without symptoms (Stage B), symptomatic HF (Stage C), and advanced disease (Stage D). [3] [4] [5] An estimated one-third of adults meet Stage A criteria, while 24-34% may meet Stage B criteria. [1] Community-based cohorts have demonstrated that asymptomatic Stage A/B disease is associated with substantial risk of progression, [6] yet identifying these stages remains challenging outside specialized research settings. [7] The concept of Stage B originated in the 2001 ACC/AHA guideline, [3] which defined this stage by the presence of structural heart disease in the absence of HF symptoms.

text.text: The 2021 First Universal Definition of HF renamed this stage "pre-HF" and expanded its diagnostic criteria to include elevated natriuretic peptides or cardiac troponins as corroborating evidence. [8] The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline subsequently incorporated this framework into U.S. clinical practice, recognizing that individuals with HF risk factors and elevated BNP or NT-proBNP, or persistently elevated cardiac troponin, may meet Stage B criteria even in the absence of imaging-confirmed structural abnormalities. [5, 8] An analysis from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study demonstrated that biomarker-based criteria reclassified approximately one in five older adults from Stage A to Stage B, identifying individuals with higher subsequent risk. [9] The 2026 Second Universal Definition reaffirmed this diagnostic pathway, while introducing greater international harmonization, designating Stage 0 for individuals without HF risk factors (corresponding to the "no apparent risk" group in this study; Table S1), and emphasizing Stage B as an opportunity for early detection. [10] Because natriuretic peptide concentrations increase with age independently of cardiac disease, the choice of diagnostic threshold, particularly fixed versus age-adjusted cutoffs, can materially influence pre-HF classification. [11] This raises the possibility that pre-HF could be operationalized using biomarkers alone, extending its identification beyond imaging-based cohorts.

text.text: However, whether explicitly incorporating biomarker criteria into a staged phenotype, rather than treating NT-proBNP solely as a continuous risk marker, meaningfully differentiates prognosis at the population level remains unclear.

Most HF epidemiologic studies rely on self-reported diagnoses, thereby primarily capturing Stage C disease, whereas natriuretic peptide studies generally evaluate these biomarkers as continuous predictors rather than components of a staged phenotype.

Although one large study demonstrated that NT-proBNP independently predicts mortality outside a formal staging framework, [12] related NHANES research examining preclinical HF, defined by conventional risk factors and prior myocardial infarction, and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality over 1999-2018 did not establish a biomarker-defined Stage B or evaluate the full HF continuum. [13] Moreover, elevated biomarkers in the absence of conventional risk factors may still indicate clinically meaningful risk but may not be adequately represented by any single conventional stage. [14] Accordingly, whether biomarker-defined Stage B constitutes a prognostically distinct phenotype relative to both no apparent risk and established HF remains unresolved. [15] NHANES provides a valuable opportunity to address this question.

text.text: Previous analyses of this biomarker substudy demonstrated that NT-proBNP was a robust predictor of mortality independent of kidney function, [17] and documented racial and ethnic differences in NT-proBNP concentrations, [18] highlighting both the feasibility and the complexities of its application in population-based research.

text.text: Collectively, these data provide an opportunity to construct a four-level phenotype comprising no apparent risk, Stage A, biomarker-defined Stage B, and self-reported Stage C, and to preliminarily evaluate its prognostic relevance.

This study aims to develop a computable, biomarker-informed phenotype of the HF continuum, aligned with consensus criteria, using NHANES and linked mortality data, and to determine whether formal staging provides prognostic information beyond a general elevation in mortality risk.

We hypothesized that the 2026 Universal Definition could be operationalized using variables available in a nationally representative health survey and that the resulting phenotypes would exhibit distinct long-term mortality trajectories, providing preliminary population-level evidence relevant to the updated staging framework.
We conducted a cohort analysis of participants from the 1999-2000, 2001-2002, and 2003-2004 NHANES cycles.

text.text: NHANES is a nationally representative, multistage survey of the noninstitutionalized U.S. population conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics.
The HF-continuum phenotype was assigned cross-sectionally at baseline, and participants were subsequently followed for mortality.
These survey cycles were selected because NT-proBNP measurements were available only during this period, in a subset of participants selected for the NHANES surplus-sera biomarker substudy.
Mortality outcomes were ascertained through linkage to the National Death Index, with follow-up time calculated from the examination date to death or administrative censoring on December 31, 2019.

The analytic framework translated the 2026 Universal Definition into a four-level phenotype: no apparent HF risk, Stage A (at risk), Stage B (elevated NT-proBNP without self-reported HF), and Stage C (self-reported HF).

text.text: Because several constructs could not be operationalized with the available data, the analysis was restricted to the four phenotypes that could be constructed and evaluated in relation to mortality.

Participants were eligible if they were aged ≥20 years at examination and had nonmissing self-reported HF status, complete examination and survey design variables, eligibility for mortality linkage, recorded follow-up time, and nonmissing core phenotype variables.
Pregnant participants were excluded.
All analyses accounted for the complex survey design, including primary sampling units and strata.

The pooled 6-year biomarker substudy weight was derived by combining two-thirds of the 1999-2002 4-year weight with one-third of the 2003-2004 2-year weight, using the appropriate weight variable for each participant's survey cycle.

Variance estimation was performed using Taylor series linearization implemented through the survey package in R. For discrimination and reclassification metrics not amenable to linearization, variance was estimated using cluster bootstrap resampling.
Stage B/pre-HF biomarker Stage B was defined using NT-proBNP concentrations measured in stored serum samples from the NHANES surplus-sera biomarker substudy.
NT-proBNP is renally cleared, and its concentrations may be lower in individuals with obesity independently of cardiac status.
Moreover, a single fixed threshold does not account for the wellestablished age-related increase in NT-proBNP concentrations.

Consistent with the general principles of the Universal Definition and threshold approaches adopted in previous studies, [19] participants were classified as Stage B if their NT-proBNP concentration exceeded the 90th percentile of an age-and sex-specific reference distribution.

text.text: This distribution was constructed using an unweighted approach across 14 strata defined by seven 10-year age groups and sex, among participants with nonmissing NT-proBNP measurements and no self-reported HF.
Percentile ranks were calculated within each stratum, with tied values assigned identical percentile ranks.
Strata containing fewer than 10 reference participants were considered insufficient for percentile estimation.
Accordingly, Stage B status was classified as missing for participants with missing NT-proBNP measurements, missing age, or membership in an undersized stratum.

These participants were excluded from the analysis unless they met the criteria for Stage C. The prevalence of Stage B in the overall cohort was not expected to equal exactly 10%, because the reference distribution was constructed without survey weighting, whereas cohort prevalence estimates incorporated the complex survey design, and because Stage B classification was restricted to participants without Stage C.
The four-level phenotype was assigned hierarchically, prioritizing Stage C over Stage B, Stage B over Stage A, and Stage A over no apparent risk (corresponding to Stage 0 in the 2026 framework).

Each participant was assigned to a single mutually exclusive category, with lower-priority stages assigned only after higher-priority criteria had been positively ruled out, rather than by default when classification at a higher level was not possible.
Stage C was defined by self-reported physician-diagnosed congestive HF on the questionnaire.
Among participants not meeting Stage B or Stage C criteria, Stage A was defined by the presence of at least one of 10 risk factors.

Eight factors-hypertension, diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease (CKD), albuminuria, prior coronary heart disease (CHD) or myocardial infarction (MI), prior stroke, and current smokingcorresponded to risk factors specified in the 2026 Universal Definition.
Age ≥65 years [20] and a composite social vulnerability indicator [21] were additionally included based on prior literature.

text.text: The latter was defined by the presence of at least one of the following: low income, low educational attainment, lack of health insurance, or absence of a usual source of healthcare.

Because social vulnerability was included among the 10 Stage A criteria, the no apparent risk group was consequently more advantaged with respect to income, education, and insurance coverage. text.text: Baseline characteristics were compared across phenotypes using survey-weighted percentages for categorical variables and survey-weighted means for continuous variables, each with corresponding 95% CIs.
Survey-weighted phenotype prevalence was further examined across age groups, sex, race and ethnicity, poverty-income ratio, CKD status, and diabetes status.
The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, ascertained through linkage to the National Death Index (NDI), with follow-up extending from the examination date to death or censoring.
Unadjusted survival across phenotypes was estimated using survey-weighted Kaplan-Meier methods.
Adjusted associations were evaluated using survey-weighted Cox proportional hazards models in a nested sequence.
Model 0 was unadjusted and characterized the overall association.
Model 1 adjusted for age, sex, and race and ethnicity.
Model 2 additionally adjusted for educational attainment, poverty-income ratio, and health insurance status.
Model 3, the primary model, further adjusted for hypertension, diabetes, obesity, CKD, smoking, and prior CHD, MI, or stroke.
NT-proBNP was not included as a covariate in any model because it was used to define Stage B and would therefore be structurally collinear with the exposure.
Pairwise comparisons among Stages A, B, and C were performed by changing the reference category and refitting Model 3.
Adjusted 10-year mortality risks were estimated through marginal standardization.
Specifically, 10-year survival probabilities were predicted for each participant under each phenotype, with all other covariates held at their observed values, and then averaged using survey weights.

These estimates represent predicted risks under hypothetical phenotype reassignment across the cohort's covariate distribution, rather than observed risks among participants currently classified within each phenotype or causal effects of changing phenotype.
Missing covariate data were addressed using multiple imputation by chained equations, generating 20 imputed datasets.
Mortality status, follow-up time, and phenotype assignment were included as fully observed predictors but were not imputed.
Cox models were fitted separately within each imputed dataset, and estimates were pooled using Rubin's rules.
Adjusted survival probabilities, restricted mean survival time (RMST), and differences in RMST relative to the no-apparent-risk group were derived from the primary model.

Incremental prognostic value was assessed by comparing a conventional threelevel phenotype without NT-proBNP against the full four-level phenotype using the Cstatistic, calibration slope, integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and continuous net reclassification improvement (NRI).

Sensitivity analyses evaluated the robustness of the findings to alternative phenotype definitions and analytical specifications, including substitution of a fixed NT-proBNP threshold for the percentile-based definition, exclusion of participants with advanced CKD based on measured estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), stratification by obesity status, complete-case analysis, use of age as the underlying time scale in Cox models, and exclusion of deaths occurring within six months of examination.
Among 31,126 participants in NHANES 1999-2004, 15,332 were aged ≥20 years, of whom 15,262 had nonmissing self-reported HF status.

Because NT-proBNP was measured only in the subset selected for the surplus-sera biomarker substudy, and valid subsample-specific survey weights were required to obtain nationally representative estimates, participants without a valid substudy weight were excluded (n = 2,998), leaving 12,264 participants.

Further exclusions were made for ineligibility for mortality linkage (n = 12), incomplete core phenotype variables (n = 125), and pregnancy at the time of examination (n = 650), resulting in a final analytic cohort of 11,477 participants (Figure 2).

Distribution of HF phenotypes Under the four-level HF classification, 1,318 participants were classified as having no apparent HF risk, 8,649 met Stage A criteria, 1,121 met Stage B criteria (elevated NT-proBNP without self-reported HF), and 389 were classified as Stage C based on selfreported HF.

Demographic and socioeconomic characteristics: Mean age increased across the HF continuum, reaching 65.6 years in Stage C, whereas sex distributions were broadly similar across phenotypes.

Racial and ethnic composition differed most notably in Stage A, which was predominantly non-Hispanic White (68.5%), consistent with this largest phenotype more closely reflecting the underlying population distribution.

Educational attainment and socioeconomic status declined progressively across phenotypes: the proportion of college graduates decreased from 46.8% in the no-apparent-risk group to 9.6% in Stage C, while mean PIR declined from 4.0 to 2.2.

Uninsured individuals accounted for 8.1% of Stage C. Fewer than 20% of participants overall reported lacking a usual source of healthcare, and full food security was most prevalent in the no-apparentrisk group (94.9%).

Cardiometabolic risk factors: Hypertension, absent by definition in the no-apparent-risk group, increased in prevalence to 65.9% in Stage C. Systolic blood pressure increased, whereas diastolic blood pressure declined across progressively advanced phenotypes, consistent with age-related widening of pulse pressure.
Diabetes prevalence was comparable between Stages A and B but increased to 29.8% in Stage C, accompanied by higher HbA1c levels.
BMI, waist circumference, and dyslipidemia were also highest in Stage C and lowest in the no-apparent-risk group.
Current smoking was most prevalent in Stages A and B but less common in Stage C despite greater cumulative tobacco exposure, potentially reflecting smoking cessation following clinical diagnosis.
Kidney function and renal markers: The prevalence of self-reported CKD and albuminuria, as well as KDIGO very-high-risk classification, increased progressively across phenotypes.

Adjusted cumulative mortality curve Hazard ratios (HRs) across HF phenotypes attenuated substantially with sequential covariate adjustment (Figure 5).

In the unadjusted model (Model 0), HRs relative to the no-apparent-risk group were 6.54 (95% CI, 4.68-9.14) for Stage A, 8.94 (95% CI, 6.48-12.34) for Stage B, and 37.43 (95% CI, 25.38-55.21) for Stage C. Adjustment for age, sex, and race and ethnicity (Model 1) reduced these estimates to 2.81, 5.60, and 6.68, respectively.
Further adjustment for educational attainment, PIR, and insurance status (Model 2) yielded HRs of 2.18, 4.26, and 4.65, respectively.

In the fully adjusted model Among the covariates in Model 3, age (HR, 1.10 per year) and current smoking (HR, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.80-2.36) exhibited the largest associations with mortality, followed by CKD (HR, 1.59), diabetes (HR, 1.54), prior stroke (HR, 1.51), and prior CHD/MI (HR, 1.18).
Hypertension and obesity were not significantly associated with mortality after adjustment.
Female sex was associated with lower mortality (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.58-0.69).
Compared with Mexican American participants, mortality was higher among non-Hispanic Black (HR, 1.41) and non-Hispanic White participants (HR, 1.32).
Higher PIR was associated with lower mortality (HR, 0.89 per unit; 95% CI, 0.86-0.93), while educational attainment exhibited a modest gradient.
Insurance status was not significantly associated with mortality.

Because the preceding HRs were each estimated relative to the no-apparent-risk group, Stages A, B, and C were additionally compared directly to characterize differences in mortality risk across the more advanced phenotypes.
Using Stage A as the reference, both Stage B (HR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.62-2.07) and Stage C (HR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.35-1.97) were associated with significantly higher mortality (both p<0.001).

text.text: Because Stages A and B were both defined among participants without self-reported HF, this comparison provides an assessment of the additional prognostic information associated with biomarker-defined Stage B relative to Stage A, independent of classification into the selfreport-dependent Stage C category.
Conversely, when Stage B was used as the reference, the comparison with Stage C showed no statistically significant difference in mortality (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.71-1.11; p=0.305) (Table 3).

Notably, the point estimate for Stage B exceeded that for Stage C, indicating that the adjusted mortality pattern did not follow a strictly monotonic progression from no apparent risk through Stages A, B, and C.

text.text: Complete-case analysis without multiple imputation (N = 10,079) and an alternative Cox model using age as the underlying time scale also produced estimates consistent with the primary findings (HR, 2.59; 95% CI, 1.96-3.43, and HR, 2.71; 95% CI, 1.88-3.92, respectively).
These findings also help reconcile an apparent discrepancy between the adjusted mortality associations and the incremental prognostic performance of the phenotype.

Although Stage B retained a significantly elevated HR in the fully adjusted model, its incorporation into the conventional model yielded only a negligible improvement in the Cstatistic (0.868 to 0.870) and an IDI estimate that was not distinguishable from zero.

The continuous NRI was nominally significant (0.219; 95% CI, 0.058-0.381); however, this metric can be sensitive to relatively small changes in predicted risk, even in the absence of meaningful improvements in discrimination.

These measures address different aspects of prognostic performance: an HR quantifies the relative mortality hazard associated with a phenotype, whereas discrimination and reclassification metrics assess whether incorporating that phenotype improves risk ranking or classification across individuals in a population.

The latter objective becomes inherently more difficult when a strong predictor, such as age, is already included in the model. [28] Collectively, these findings support the prognostic relevance of biomarker-defined Stage B beyond conventional predictors but do not establish this particular operational phenotype as a validated clinical entity.

text.text: An important related question-whether categorical staging of NT-proBNP provides additional prognostic information beyond its use as a continuous biomarkerwas not directly evaluated and warrants further investigation.

The association between Stage B and all-cause mortality was directionally consistent and of broadly similar magnitude across alternative analytical specifications, including use of a fixed NT-proBNP threshold, exclusion of participants with advanced CKD, exclusion of early deaths, complete-case analysis, and use of age as the underlying time scale in Cox models.
One potential exception emerged in the obesity-stratified analysis, in which the association appeared modestly weaker among participants with obesity.
However, the confidence intervals overlapped substantially, and no formal test for interaction was performed.

A plausible explanation is the well-documented inverse relationship between obesity and circulating natriuretic peptide concentrations, reported since at least the mid-2000s and potentially attributable to reduced cardiac production, altered peptide clearance, or both. [29, 30] Consequently, applying a population-based percentile threshold may result in lower sensitivity for identifying biomarker-defined Stage B among individuals with obesity.

There are several limitations.
First, the phenotype is a proxy-based approximation of the 2026 Universal Definition, with important limitations in stage assignment.
Elevated NT-proBNP alone cannot establish pre-HF, as elevations may reflect noncardiac conditions.

A related NHANES analysis using risk factor-based preclinical HF definitions reported stronger associations with cardiovascular than allcause mortality, suggesting that our endpoint may underestimate cardiovascular-specific associations.[13] However, cause-specific analyses require validated cardiovascular death classification and appropriate competing-risk methods, as noncardiovascular death precludes subsequent cardiovascular death.[35]

text.text: This study examined whether the 2026 Universal Definition of Heart Failure could be operationalized as a computable, biomarker-informed phenotype using a nationally representative U.S. health survey and whether the resulting classification provided meaningful prognostic information.

Using self-reported HF status, measured NT-proBNP, and conventional cardiometabolic risk factors from NHANES, we constructed a four-level HF-continuum phenotype that stratified long-term all-cause mortality risk.
The highest mortality risks were observed in Stages B and C, which exhibited HRs of similar magnitude after full covariate adjustment.

Stage B remained independently associated with mortality after adjustment, and its association was not fully attenuated by the covariates that accounted for much of the excess mortality associated with Stage C. However, incorporating Stage B into a conventional risk model yielded only marginal improvements in discrimination, highlighting the distinction between an independent prognostic association and incremental improvement in population-level risk stratification.
